String.Text:
Provides functionality to listen to changes in Octane's node system or force an update after making a set of changes.

An observer can be used to observe either item changes or time changes. The observer must be in scope to receive the events.

Example usage:

-- Create a new observer.
myObserver = createObserver({itemChangeCallback = myCallback}).

-- Start observing an item.
octane.changemanager.observeItem(item, myObserver, eventMask)

-- Observe a second item, using the same callback.
octane.changemanager.observeItem(otherItem, myObserver, eventMask)

-- Stop observing a particular item.
octane.changemanager.stopItemObserver(myObserver, item)

-- Stop observing all items.
octane.changemanager.stopItemObserver(myObserver)
Properties for an item change event.
Properties for a time change event.

Updates all previous changes. When making changes in nodes it's necessary to call this function to propagate the changes in Octane. Doing this allows to modify multiple nodes and propagate the changes only once.

true if they're equal, false otherwise

the value of the property or nil if there is no such property

Registers a callback for receiving change events for an item. If the callback is already registered, the flags from the given event mask will be added to the existing event mask.
The item that should be observed. It must be a valid node or nodegraph.
The observer interested in receiving change events.

Arranges its child components into a resizable grid layout. The grid itself is not visible. The grid arranges cells in rows or columns. Cells can be empty or components can occupy multiple grid cells. Cells can also contain nested grids.

The grid can stretch beyond its initial size but it cannot shrink beyond its initial size. You should setup the grid with the minimum initial size of the components.

A grid layout can only be added to a window via the gridLayout property.

Here's a usage example of the grid layout:

local layout = octane.gridlayout.create()
layout:startSetup()
 local row = 1

 local title = octane.gui.create{ type=octane.componentType.TITLE_COMPONENT, text="Settings" }
 layout:add(title, 1, row)
 row = row + 1

 local button1 = octane.gui.create{ type=octane.componentType.BUTTON, text="First button" }
 layout:add(button1, 1, row)
 row = row + 1

 local button2 = octane.gui.create{ type=octane.componentType.BUTTON, text="Second button" }
 layout:add(button2, 1, row)
 row = row + 1

 layout:setElasticityForAllRows(0)
layout:endSetup()

local window = octane.gui.create
{

Dispatches GUI events until the given time has elapsed. This can be used to make the GUI appear responsive while doing heavy work. The timeout should be small, in most cases it can be less than 100 milliseconds.

This function should be used with care. You may receive callbacks while this function is running, like GUI callbacks, render callbacks or timer callbacks. If any of these callbacks open a dialog window, this function will not return until that window is closed, regardless of the timeout.

Due to the complications above, this function should not be used to run code after a set delay, use octane.timer instead.

Binds a component's property to data in the property table. When a component's property and data are bound, updating the data value updates the property and updating the component updates the data value. A callback is called when the data value is updated from the user interface. This function will throw an error when the property is not bindable or doesn't exist. Converts a matrix into rotation/scale/translation. Only orthogonal matrices can be represented (more or less) exactly by these 3 vectors. There are currently 3 ways to write Lua code in OCTANE_PRODUCT_NAME: In a Lua script, in a Lua script graph and in a render job graph. You will find more details about those below.

In general, you can use all functionality of the Lua language (OCTANE_PRODUCT_NAME uses currently version 5.3) as well as additional functions provided by OCTANE_PRODUCT_NAME to interact with Octane, the project and rendering.

The Lua documentation portal can be found under the URL:
 https://www.lua.org/docs.html
And the Lua 5.3 reference manual can be found here:
 https://www.lua.org/manual/5.3

The Lua API of OCTANE_PRODUCT_NAME is documented in the Lua API browser (which you are using right now).

Another source of information are the Lua scripts and render jobs distributed with the Standalone.

And last but not least you can find a lot of valuable information and exisiting scripts on our dedicated Lua scripting forum:
 https://render.otoy.com/forum/viewforum.php?f=73


=== LUA SCRIPTS ===

Lua scripts can be either written directly in the Lua script editor and run from there. Or you create a file with suffix .lua in the Lua script directory that is set in the application preferences. All scripts in that directory will appear in the script menu.

To run a Lua script you either select it from the script menu or you select it in the Lua script editor and click on the run button. Alternatively you can assign a keyboard shortcut via the metadata section (see below) and run the script this way.


=== LUA SCRIPT GRAPHS ===

Lua script graphs allow you to add new functionality to the node system of OCTANE_PRODUCT_NAME. Examples would be a script graph that allows you to switch between multiple inputs or a script graph that moves a camera along a circle.

Fundamentally a Lua script graph consists of a special node graph with an assigned Lua script. This script can then create inputs and outputs of the node graph and any other node items it needs. Then whenever the time or its inputs are changed it can update the content of the node graph.

For more information about writing a Lua script graph please read the documentation of the module "scriptgraph" in the Lua API browser.

To create a new Lua script graph, select "Other" -> "Scripted graph" in the item dropdown menu of the node graph editor. Then start writing the Lua code.

To reuse finished Lua script graphs you can either export it into a ORBX package or store it in the Local DB. Alternatively, you can add a defined category in the metadata (see below) of the Lua script and save the Lua script in the Lua script directory. After re-scanning the folder, the Lua script graph will appear as an option in the new item context menu.


=== RENDER JOB GRAPHS ===

Render job graphs are a Lua script graphs with additional callbacks so that they can be integrated into the render job render flow. For more information please consult the documentation of the module "renderjobgraph" or check out the examples we distribute with the Standalone.


=== METADATA ===

In the header of a Lua script you can define additional metadata to help the user and allow a better integration of the Lua script in the OCTANE_PRODUCT_NAME user interface.

These are the possible fields you can define:

@author - Author(s) of the script.

@description - Short description of the script and what it does.

@version - Version of the script.

@script-id - A string unique to this script, used to identify stored script settings and data. See storage module for more details.
Not valid for Lua script graphs and render job graphs.

@shortcut - Shortcut key to execute the script. The shortcut should specify a key plus an optional modifier, e.g "ALT + S". The list of assigned shortcuts can be found in tab "Shortcuts" of the OCTANE_PRODUCT_NAME application preferences.
Not valid for Lua script graphs and render job graphs.

@node-registry-category - Category under which a Lua script graph registers in the node registry. Must start with "|" followed by any categories and the name under which the script graph should appear in the node graph context menu. For example,
"|My script graphs|Awesome graphs|Make movie"
will appear in the category "My script graphs" -> "Awesome graphs" with the menu entry "Make movie".
Valid only for Lua script graphs.

String.Text:
The render job graph is a special type of script graph, with additional features to support us with the render functions(Eg: Batch render).

The main purpose of this render job will be that the render settings can be saved with the project. The render job graph will also allow us with additional options like creating multiple render job nodes for different settings

Batch render job, Daylight animation job, Turntable animation job scripts are shipped with OCTANE_PRODUCT_NAME. These render job graphs can be created from the node graph editor context menu.

Script:

Please read the script graph to find out, how to use Lua script in the script graph.

The attributes of the render job graph listed under GT_RENDER_JOB, this can be viewed in the items window.
Two important attributes of the render job graph are described below.

1. A_TOTAL_FRAMES (write) : 
 The script has to specify a total number of the frames exists in this render job. The number should be grand total count of all the render target animation frames (ie if animation frames = 30 and input render target count is 3 then total frames for this render job is 90)
 Eg: graph:setAttribute(octane.A_TOTAL_FRAMES, 90)

2. A_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY (read) :
 Location on the disk where we need to save the rendered files. This is set from the render job user interface.
 Eg: graph:getAttribute(octane.A_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY)

Additional callbacks:

In addition to the script graph OnInit(), onEvaluate(), OnShutdown(), this render job graph has four additional callback functions.

onIterate, onSaveRenderedFrame, onStartIteration, onFinishIteration

For detailed description, please click on the callbacks names listed in the members window

Callback function, This is the main render loop callback function, which will be called for A_TOTAL_FRAMES times. Then this callback can tell octane viewport, which render target has to be rendered.\n
Frame index, will be in [0, A_TOTAL_FRAMES)
Render target to render, if nil the rendering will be aborted. Can be nil in case skipFrame is set to true
If true, render job will skip the render of current frame and jumps to next frame
This callback function will be called when the rendering of current frame has been completed. \n
set whether the save is successful. If false, the rendering will be aborted
This callback function is called once on the start of the iteration. The function can be used to initialize before the start of rendering.\n
This callback function is called once at the end of the iteration. It can be used to release anything upon the completion of rendering.\n
Initialize this key to a string to give your scripted graph a more meaningful default name.\n\nChanging this value after your script returns the table has no effect.
Initialize this key to an image to give your scripted graph a custom icon.\n\nAfter the script returns the table, this key is cleared, and changing it has no effect.

Stores the settings for this script specific to the node item. This table will be added to the table returned from the graph script, and it will be saved when the scene file is saved. Settings stored in this table have the same limitations as settings in the tables in the storage module.\n\nLike saving nodes, it's not possible to directly save this data when the user has opened a package.
Table with information about a scripted graph bool pin.

Callback which is called after initializing the scripted graph. Can be overridden in your script object.\n\nThis callback will be run once after updating the script and before the call to evaluate. The graph will be cleared of all nodes except the linker nodes and the special input node before this call.
true if the initialization finished without errors.

Callback which is called when the connected value of one of the input linker nodes changes. Can be overridden in your script object.

The graph is not cleared before this callback runs, all nodes created by previous calls to init and evaluate will still be there.

If onEvaluate raises an error, onShutdown will be called and no further callbacks will be received.

Callback which is called before the scripted graph is destroyed, or before the script is reloaded. Can be overridden in your script object.

If the onInit callback didn't raise an error this callback will be called once before destroying the object. You should release any external resources used by the script in this function.

You should not interact with the node graph contents during this function as the nodes connected to the inputs may have been deleted at this point, and saving the project has happened before this call.

Callback which is called when the trigger button has been clicked. The trigger button will be displayed in the node inspector if onTrigger() is provided in the script object.

The graph is not cleared before this callback runs, all nodes created by previous calls to init and evaluate will still be there.

If onTrigger() raises an error, onShutdown() will be called and no further callbacks will be received.

Resets the node graph contents to the initial state, as it would be just before init was called. This state will always still contain all linker nodes and may contain some other nodes which are internally created and used by the scripted node graph. Any other nodes added by the script will be deleted.

Assigns a new node pin info to an input linker node. Must be called only from the init or evaluate function, and can't be called for an input which was changed before this evaluate call. The given pin type must match the type of the existing linker node.

A table that defines the ID+label pairs that are shown in the enum drop-down menu. You have 2 options to define those and in both cases the entries in the drop-down menu are in the same order as in the table:
1) An array of strings, where the Lua array index (starting at 1) is used as enum ID and the string as label. For example,
 enum={"Apples", "Pears", "Bananas"}
defines an enum label list (in that order) of
 1: "Apples"
 2: "Pears"
 3: "Bananas"
2) An array of tables, where each table is an array defining the key-value pair. For example,
 enum={ { 1, "Apples" }, { 3, "Bananas" }, { 2, "Pears" } }
defines an enum label list (in that order) of
 1: "Apples"
 3: "Bananas"
 2: "Pears"

This module gives access to permanent storage of settings and data. Depending on how a script is run it may contain one or more tables whose content is persistent between subsequent executions of a script.

 To have persistent storage available the script must declare a script id in the header as follows:

-- @script-id <id>

The script ID can be any text string, but it should be unlikely that other scripts use the same ID.

The data types which can be stored permanently in these tables are the following:
Keys can be numbers and strings;
values can be numbers, booleans, strings and tables. Tables stored as values are subject to the same limitations.
Stores the application-wide settings for this script. Available in all scripts with a valid script id
Stores the project-wide settings for this script. Available in scripts with a valid script id, but not in scripted graphs.

Specifies how objects on the mesh should be imported as object layers. This attribute is ignored when loading a mesh from Alembic.

- GEOIMP_HIDE_OBJECT_LAYERS: Don't create any object layer inputs. An object layer map node will be needed to specify object layer settings.

- GEOIMP_LOAD_AS_ONE_OBJECT_LAYER: Create a single object layer input with the name "Object layer".

- GEOIMP_LOAD_ALL_OBJECT_LAYERS: Create an object layer input for every entry in A_OBJECT_NAMES. If the array attribute is empty, a single object layer input with the name "Object layer" is created.

Can be set to TRUE if the geometry has a constant topology. This means the connectivity between faces, edges and vertices stays the same during the animation of this geometry. If TRUE Octane may try to calculate motion blur from the motion of vertices between frames. This applies to polygons, hair and sphere primitives.
An array of the number of vertices for each polygon in the polygon sequence. Can only be left empty if the mesh node doesn't contain any polygons.

An array of polygon vertex positions. Can only be left empty if the mesh node doesn't contain any polygons. Animated vertices are only taken into account for motion blur if A_CONSTANT_TOPOLOGY is set to TRUE and A_POLY_VERTEX_SPEED is empty.
An array that stores the indices into A_VERTICES and A_POLY_VERTEX_SPEED for each vertex of each polygon. Its size must be equal to the sum of all vertex counts in A_VERTICES_PER_POLY.

An array of vertex speeds. If given, these speeds are used for rendering motion blur. Otherwise motion blur will be calculated from the animation of the A_VERTICES array if A_CONSTANT_TOPOLOGY is set to TRUE.

An array of vertex normals. If not empty, but A_POLY_NORMAL_INDICES is empty this array must directly store the normals for each vertex of each polygon. If left empty, the vertex normals will be calculated on-the-fly. To calculate the vertex normals the geometry import preferences as well as the smooth groups (if specified) will be used. When only some vertices have explicit vertex normals, the other vertex normals should be set to (0,0,0).
An array that stores the indices into A_NORMALS for each vertex of each polygon. Must be either empty or its size must be equal to the sum of all vertex counts in A_VERTICES_PER_POLY.

If A_NORMALS is empty and the vertex normals will be calculated on-the-fly, you can specify a smooth group for each polygon. The edges between different smooth groups will not be smoothed. Also all polygons with a negative smooth group will not be smoothed at all. If not empty, the size of this array must be equal to the size of A_VERTICES_PER_POLY.

An array of UVW coordinates. If empty, every vertex will have a UVW coordinate of (0,0,0). If not empty, but A_POLY_UVW_INDICES is empty, this array must directly store the UVW coordinates for each vertex of each polygon, i.e. its size must be the sum of all elements of A_VERTICES_PER_POLY.
An array that stores the indices into A_UVWS for each vertex of each polygon.Must be either empty or its size must be equal to the sum of all vertex counts in A_VERTICES_PER_POLY.
Defines the second set of UV coordinates. If a mesh defines the UVW2 coordinates only for some of its vertices, set the other vertices to (0,0,0).
An array that stores the indices into A_UVWS_2 for each vertex of each polygon. Must be either empty or its size must be equal to the sum of all vertex counts in A_VERTICES_PER_POLY.
Defines the third set of UV coordinates. If a mesh defines the UVW3 coordinates only for some of its vertices, set the other vertices to (0,0,0).
An array that stores the indices into A_UVWS_3 for each vertex of each polygon. Must be either empty or its size must be equal to the sum of all vertex counts in A_VERTICES_PER_POLY.
An array of material names, which must not contain duplicates. If left empty, a default material name will be used.
An array of object names, which must not contain duplicates. If left empty, a default object name will be used.

An array that stores for each polygon the assigned material via an index into A_MATERIAL_NAMES.\nThe size must be equal to the number of polygons, i.e. equal to the size of A_VERTICES_PER_POLY, or zero. If the size is zero, then a material index of 0 is used for all polygons.

An array that stores for each polygon the assigned object via an index into A_OBJECT_NAMES.\nThe size must be equal to the number of polygons, i.e. equal to the size of A_VERTICES_PER_POLY, or zero. If the size is zero, then an object index of 0 is used for all polygons.
An array that stores the number of joints influencing the corresponding vertex. Can be empty, otherwise its size must match the number of vertices in A_VERTICES.

An array that stores the IDs of all joints influencing a vertex. Its size must be equal to the sum of all joint counts in A_POLY_JOINT_COUNTS.\n The given IDs are used to match a joint node and weight to a vertex at skeletal deformation time. The IDs should match with the joint node's A_INDEX attribute.
An array that stores the weights for each joint in A_POLY_JOINT_INDICES. Its size must be equal to the size of A_POLY_JOINT_INDICES. Weights are in the range [0,1].
Inverse bind transform per joint for skinning.
An array that stores the indices into for A_REST_MATRIX for each joint. Its size must be equal to the sum of all joints counts in A_POLY_JOINT_COUNTS
An array of the number of vertices for each hair in the hair sequence. Can be empty if there is no hair in this geometry.
An array of vertex positions. Animated vertices are only taken into account for motion blur if A_CONSTANT_TOPOLOGY is set to TRUE and A_HAIR_VERTEX_SPEED is empty.
An array of vertex speeds. If given these speeds are used for rendering motion blur. Otherwise the animation of the A_HAIR_VERTICES array may be used.
An array of thickness (diameter) for every hair vertex. Must either have size 1, or the same size as the A_HAIR_VERTICES array. If the size is 1 all the hairs have the same width.
An array of 1 UV coordinate per hair. Must be either empty or have the same size as A_VERTICES_PER_HAIR. If empty, (0, 0) will be used for all hair primitives.

An array of 2 W coordinates per hair vertex which represents the position in the gradient (from 0 to 1) for the segment ending (X) and starting at it (Y). Must be either empty or have the same size as A_HAIR_VERTICES. If empty the interpolation will be done using the values specified by A_HAIR_INTERPOLATION.
Specifies the hair interpolation type of enum type HairInterpolationType. This is ignored if A_HAIR_WS is not empty.

An array that stores for each hair strand the assigned material via an index into A_MATERIAL_NAMES.\nThe size must be equal to the number of hair strands, i.e. equal to the size of A_VERTICES_PER_HAIR, or zero. If the size is zero, then a material index of 0 is used for all hair strands.

An array that stores for each hair strand the assigned object via an index into A_OBJECT_NAMES.\nThe size must be equal to the number of hair strands, i.e. equal to the size of A_VERTICES_PER_HAIR, or zero. If the size is zero, then an object index of 0 is used for all hair strands.

An array that stores the center point for each sphere primitive. Animated sphere center positions are only taken into account for motion blur if A_CONSTANT_TOPOLOGY is set to TRUE and A_SPHERE_SPEED is empty.
An array of speed vectors, one for each sphere primitive. If given these speeds are used for rendering motion blur. Otherwise the animation of the A_SPHERE_CENTERS array may be used.
A radius for each sphere primitive. Must either have size 1, or the same size as A_SPHERE_CENTERS. If the size is 1 all the spheres will have the same width.

An array that stores for each sphere the assigned material via an index into A_MATERIAL_NAMES.\nThe size must be equal to the number of spheres, i.e. equal to the size of A_SPHERE_CENTERS, or zero. If the size is zero, then a material index of 0 is used for all spheres.

An array that stores for each sphere the assigned object via an index into A_OBJECT_NAMES.\nThe size must be equal to the number of spheres, i.e. equal to the size of A_SPHERE_CENTERS, or zero. If the size is zero, then an object index of 0 is used for all spheres.
An array with 1 uv-coordinate per sphere primitive. Array must be either empty or have the same size as A_SPHERE_CENTERS. If empty, each sphere has uv-coordinate (0,0).
The indices of the corners for which the sharpness is given by A_SUBD_CORNER_SHARPNESS
Corner sharpness. The length must be equal to the length of A_SUBD_CORNER_INDICES

The indices into the A_VERTICES array for every vertex of every semi-sharp edge.\nIf A_SUBD_CREASE_LENGTH is empty: the length is be even, and every pair of indices defines a semi-sharp edge in the mesh.\nIf A_SUBD_CREASE_LENGTH is not empty: every element L in If A_SUBD_CREASE_LENGTH defines a chain of (L-1) semi-sharp edges. This array contains L indices specifying the vertices in the chain.
Optional, see A_SUBD_CREASE_INDICES description. If given, all elements must be >= 2.
Crease sharpness. Contains one value for every semi-sharp edge.

String.Text: Defines the length unit used to interpret the worldbounds of the volume. (see Octane::GeometryImportScale)
Isovalue used when converting between fog volumes and levelsets.
Amount of voxels that will be generated on either side of the surface (outside, inside) when loading a mesh or a fog volume as an SDF volume.
Name of the grid in a VDB to load for absorption. If an empty string is provided then no grid will be loaded. If the grid cannot be found in the VDB, then no grid will be loaded.
This scalar value scales the grid value used for absorption.
Name of the grid in a VDB to load for scattering. If an empty string is provided then no grid will be loaded. If the grid cannot be found in the VDB, then no grid will be loaded.
This scalar value scales the grid value used for scattering.

Name of the grid in a VDB to load for providing temperature information. If an empty string is provided then no grid will be loaded. If the grid cannot be found in the VDB, then no grid will be loaded.
This scalar value scales the grid value used for temperature. Use this when temperature information in a grid is too low.

Name of a vec3s type grid in the VDB to load for motion blur. If specified then this will take precedence over A_VOLUME_VELOCITY_ID_*. If specified when exporting from a regular grid to a VDB, then the exported VDB will contain a vec3s grid for velocities. If not, then the exporter will check whether the A_VOLUME_VELOCITY_ID_* attributes are set, and if so, it will export individual component grids.

Name of a float grid in the VDB to use for the x-component of motion blur vectors. If A_VOLUME_VELOCITY_ID_* are all set to non-empty strings, when exporting from a regular grid, and A_VOLUME_VELOCITY_ID is set to an empty string, then the exporter will create independent velocity component grids in the VDB.

Name of a float grid in the VDB to use for the y-component of motion blur vectors. If A_VOLUME_VELOCITY_ID_* are all set to non-empty strings, when exporting from a regular grid, and A_VOLUME_VELOCITY_ID is set to an empty string, then the exporter will create independent velocity component grids in the VDB.

Name of a float grid in the VDB to use for the z-component of motion blur vectors. If A_VOLUME_VELOCITY_ID_* are all set to non-empty strings, when exporting from a regular grid, and A_VOLUME_VELOCITY_ID is set to an empty string, then the exporter will create independent velocity component grids in the VDB.
This scalar value linearly scales velocity vectors in the velocity grid.

The names of the grids to load. The grid names specified via usage specific attributes like A_VOLUME_SCATTER_ID will be added automatically if necessary. Standard Volume mediums support per-instance channel assignments and can select any of the grids loaded for the volume.
Hierarchical tree leaves for the volume.
Hierarchical tree nodes for the volume.
This zero-based offset specifies which float inside a voxel is applied to absorption. If negative, it will be assumed that the channel is disabled.
The maximum float value in the absorption channel's grid. This value is calculated automatically.
The default background absorption value of the volume. Usually 0.
This zero-based offset specifies which float inside a voxel is applied to scattering. If negative, it will be assumed that the channel is disabled.
The maximum float value in the scatter channel's grid. This value is calculated automatically.
This zero-based offset specifies which float inside a voxel is applied to emission. If negative, it will be assumed that the channel is disabled.
The maximum float value in the emission channel's grid. This value is calculated automatically.
The default background emission value for the volume. Usually 0.
This zero-based offset specifies the channel index (offset inside a singlevoxel) to be used for the velocity vector x-component.
This zero-based offset specifies the channel index (offset inside a singlevoxel) to be used for the velocity vector y-component.
This zero-based offset specifies the channel index (offset inside a singlevoxel) to be used for the velocity vector z-component.
The default background velocity value for this volume. Usually (0,0,0).

These zero-based offsets specify the first float in a voxel referenced by the channel at the corresponding index in A_VOLUME_CHANNEL_IDS. If negative, it will be assumed that the respective channel is disabled. When importing a VDB, this array will be populated automatically, but when loading a grid via A_VOLUME_REGULAR_GRID, then the size of this array must match the size of A_VOLUME_CHANNEL_IDS.
The maximum float values in the channels corresponding to A_VOLUME_CHANNEL_IDS. These will be determined automatically.

The default background values for the channels corresponding to A_VOLUME_CHANNEL_IDS. Usually (0, 0, 0). When importing a VDB, this array will be populated automatically, but when loading a grid via A_VOLUME_REGULAR_GRID, then the size of this array must match the size of A_VOLUME_CHANNEL_IDS.

A bool array to indicate if the channels corresponding to A_VOLUME_CHANNEL_IDS provide a single float (false) or a float3 (true) per voxel. When importing a VDB, this array will be populated automatically, but when loading a grid via A_VOLUME_REGULAR_GRID, then the size of this array must match the size of A_VOLUME_CHANNEL_IDS.

Voxels are stored in order of x-axis, followed by rows up the y-axis, then finally, it repeats for each z-slice. If you have more than one float per voxel, then store each voxel as a set of floats contiguously. After that you set A_VOLUME_ABSORPTION_OFFSET, A_VOLUME_SCATTER_OFFSET, A_VOLUME_EMISSION_OFFSET and A_VOLUME_VELOCITY_OFFSET_{XYZ} to an integer index into your voxels. For example, if you have 2 floats in each voxel, and the second float is what you want for scatter, then you set A_VOLUME_SCATTER_OFFSET to 1.

 Optionally, you can also provide the A_VOLUME_CHANNEL_{IDS, OFFSETS, DEFAULTS, IS_FLOAT3} array attributes to load additional named channels for use with standard volume mediums. The floats of any float3 channel must be stored in consecutive indices of the voxel.

 You must provide at least one valid offset. Finally, set A_VOLUME_RESOLUTION to the number of voxels in each dimension. The volume at this point is set in space with each voxel measuring 1m x 1m x 1m. To change the scale, you can set A_TRANSFORM.
The voxel size in floats for the volume channel data stored in each voxel. This will be set automatically.
(deprecated) This zero-based offset specifies the index into the voxels of the first float of three floats comprising a motion vector for the voxel.

The user ID of this geometry node. A valid ID should be a non-negative number. It's a non-unique ID attribute, multiple geometry nodes can have same ID, so it's a user responsibility to set unique ID if needed. In a tree hierarchy, the ID of current node will override the input geometry node's ID
Raw byte uncompressed data for the image.
Size of the image in pixels or if the image is compressed the size of the image in blocks.
The image type, i.e. the data format used in A_BUFFER. Must be of type ImageType.
The original type of the image file, i.e. the data format stored in the image file.
True if the image can wrap around in the horizontal direction, false otherwise.
True if the image can wrap around in the vertical direction, false otherwise.

True if the rows of pixels are stored in the buffer starting with the top row of the image and going down, false if they are stored starting with the bottom row of the image and going up. If A_TYPE is a compressed type, this must be true.
Information about the image source (file), which is used only in the UI.
Will contain the layer names if the image was loaded from a file that contained layers. Will be empty otherwise.

Indicates the channel format to be used after conversion and compression:
 - IMAGE_CHANNEL_FLOAT: use float for HDR images, and uint8 for LDR images.
 - IMAGE_CHANNEL_HALF or IMAGE_CHANNEL_UINT8: use half for HDR images, and uint8 for LDR images.
 - IMAGE_CHANNEL_AUTO: use float or half depending on the source image data (if the source is half precision float or 16-bit integer data, then load as half) for HDR images, and uint8 for LDR images.
 - other types: compress the loaded image.
Indicate the chosen layer name, if the current image has multiple layers.

Stores the geometry archive file to load. Currently Alembic, FBX and GLTF files are supported. To load a new file, just change this attribute and evaluate the node graph. Too large a value will produce an overly blurry result without fine details. Too small a value will reduce the maximum possible strength of the bloom.

The action is stored in the first component of the vector and the input index in the second.\nThe input with index 0 is at the beginning of the dynamic pin list.\nAfter evaluation the attribute will be reset to { INPUT_ACTION_NONE, 0 }.

Whether to apply the postfx media rendering settings on the final AOV output. Only used if this node is the root output AOV node (i.e. directly connected to the AOV output group node).

String.Text: Whether this layer is applied or skipped.
When selected, this layer modifies the input of the next lower layer that is not itself attached to a layer. Otherwise, it applies to the output of the next lower layer.
The opacity channel used to control the transparency of this layer.
The blend mode used to mix the RGB values of this layer with those of the background.
The alpha compositing operation used to combine the blend result with the background.
The channels to which to apply the operation (others are left unmodified).

In pass-through mode, this is a non-isolated compositing group. Its background is the output of the layers below it.\n\nWhen disabled, this is an isolated compositing group. Its background is black and fully transparent.
Clamp the result of blending each layer to [0,1] (ignored when used as a normal map).
The background color is gray (0.7) instead of black if the bottom layer is disconnected. The "Texture" layer inputs are clamped in addition to the blend results if "Clamp" is enabled.
Whether this material is applied or skipped.
Material input of one layer. The materials are sorted bottom to top, i.e. "Material 1" is the bottom-most material.
Input map that determines the opacity of the corresponding material input. "Material 1 mask" will be ignored.
The number of materials to mix. Three pins per new material are created and appended to the end.
Reduces burned out highlights by compressing them and reducing their contrast.
Controls the extent to which clipping is done per channel.
OCIO view that produces sRGB output.

How smoothly to compress highlights to prevent clipping. 0.0 means hard clipping (no rolloff). Values larger than about 1.0 will start to noticeably darken midtones; at that point consider reducing exposure instead.
If enabled, saturation of bright colors will be sacrificed to preserve more luminance information. If disabled, saturation will always be preserved at the expense of luminance.

How smoothly to transition from increased input luminance causing increased output luminance to increased input luminance causing decreased output saturation instead. 0.0 means a hard transition (where maximum saturation is achieved at the cost of a noticeable discontinuity). Too-large values will just decrease overall saturation.\n\nThis only has an effect when Desaturate highlights is enabled.
Mix amount between the first and second texture.

String.Text: The type of Cryptomatte render AOV from which to extract mattes.

List of selected matte names, one per line.

Some characters have special meaning:
 * is a wildcard that matches any sequence of characters.
 - at the start of a line excludes any mattes matched by that line.
 ? on a line by itself matches mattes with blank names.
 \ prevents the next character being treated as a special character.

Blank lines are ignored. When a matte name is included by one line and excluded by another, whichever line comes last takes precedence. For example,
 Car_*
 -*dirt*
 Car_wheel_dirt
will include "Car_windows" and "Car_wheel_dirt", but not "Ground" or "Car_door_dirt".

String.Text: The type of curvature to sample.
Specifies the maximum area affected by the curvature effect.
Determines the proportion of the maximum area affected by the curvature effect.
Specifies the offset from the surface used to sample the neighbouring geometry.
Tolerance for small curvature and small angles between polygons.

Spread controls the ray direction with respect to the normal of the surface. 0 means curvature is sampled straight in the direction of the surface normal, and 1 means the sampling rays are shot perpendicular to the surface normal.

Includes objects when calculating the curvature value: By default the selected mode is All, which includes all object intersections into calculating curvature. If Self is selected, then only self-intersection is taken into account for curvature. If Others is selected, then only ray-intersection with other objects is used for curvature.
Preserve hue and saturation|Inflated maximum channel (smooth)
Preserve hue and saturation|Luminance (before tone mapping only)
Preserve hue, shift saturation|Maximum and minimum channels
Preserve hue, shift saturation|Inflated maximum and minimum channels (smooth)
Shift hue and saturation|Individual RGB channels

The control points (x = input value, y = output value) of the curve (or the primary sub curve when "all channels" mode is being used).\n\nThese must be sorted by x value (strictly increasing), with all x and y values >= 0. There must be no more than 64 points.

The control points (x = input value, y = output value) of the secondary sub curve to be applied to the red channel after the primary sub curve is. This is only meaningful when "all channels" mode is being used.\n\nThese must be sorted by x value (strictly increasing), with all x and y values >= 0. There must be no more than 64 points.

The control points (x = input value, y = output value) of the secondary sub curve to be applied to the green channel after the primary sub curve is. This is only meaningful when "all channels" mode is being used.\n\nThese must be sorted by x value (strictly increasing), with all x and y values >= 0. There must be no more than 64 points.

The control points (x = input value, y = output value) of the secondary sub curve to be applied to the blue channel after the primary sub curve is. This is only meaningful when "all channels" mode is being used.\n\nThese must be sorted by x value (strictly increasing), with all x and y values >= 0. There must be no more than 64 points.
Set it to TRUE if the file needs a reload. After the node was evaluated the attribute will be false again.

Vector which defines the direction from which the sun is shining.
Sky turbidity, i.e. the amount of sun light that is scattered. A high value will reduce the contrast between objects in the shadow and in sun light.

Scale factor that is applied to the sun only. Use this to adjust the relative power of the sun compared to the sky.\n\nNote: values other than 1.0 can produce unrealistic results because in the real world the sky is lit by the sun. Adjusting the balance between the yellowish sun and the bluish sky can also produce a hue shift in the scene.

Use environment texture instead of the sky.
Use importance sampling for image textures.
If photon mapping is used, cast photons from bright sources in the environment map.
The medium in the environment (free space). Ignored when this environment is used as a the visible environment.
Radius of the environment medium. The environment medium acts as a sphere around the camera position with the specified radius.
Enable or disable this daylight environment in post volume rendering.
When used as a visible environment, this environment will behave as a backplate image.
When used as a visible environment, this environment will be visible in reflections (specular and glossy materials).
When used as a visible environment, this environment will be visible in refractions.
The slope of bump maps is calculated slightly differently, making it more sensitive to the orientation of the UV mapping.
The diffuse color of the material.
The transmission color of the material.
Bump channel to simulate a relief using a grayscale texture interpreted as height map for the layer.
The height represented by a normalized value of 1.0 in the bump texture. 0 disables bump mapping, negative values will invert the bump map.
Normal channel to distort normals of the layer using an RGB image.
Opacity channel controlling the transparency of the layer via grayscale texture.
Diffuse transmission channel which can be used for thin translucent objects.
Diffuse roughness to allow simulation of very rough surfaces like sand or clay.
Medium inside the material if transmission is used.
Opacity channel controlling the transparency of the material via grayscale texture.
Bump channel to simulate a relief using a grayscale texture interpreted as height map.
Normal channel to distort normals using an RGB image.
Displacement channel to create highly detailed geometry.
If disabled normal interpolation will be disabled and triangle meshes will appear "facetted".
If enabled self-intersecting shadow terminator for low polygon is smoothed according to the polygon's curvature.
Smooth sharp edges during render time.

Switches the material to a shadow catcher, i.e. it will be transparent unless there is some (direct) shadow cast onto the material, which will make it less transparent depending on the shadow strength.
Material layer above this base material.
(deprecated) Radius of rounded edges that are rendered as shading effect.
The number of samples per pixel that will be calculated before rendering is stopped.
Determines how global illumination is approximated.
The maximum path depth for which specular reflections/refractions are allowed.
The maximum path depth for which glossy reflections are allowed.
The maximum path depth for which diffuse reflections are allowed.
How much space to allocate for overlapping volumes. Ray marching is faster with low values but you can get artefacts where lots of volumes overlap.
Maximum distance for environment ambient occlusion.
Ambient occlusion environment texture, which is used for AO rays. If not specified, the environment will be used instead.
Enables direct light through opacity maps. If disabled, ray tracing will be faster but renders incorrect shadows for alpha-mapped geometry or specular materials with "fake shadows" enabled.
Enables nested dielectrics. If disabled, the surface IORs not tracked and surface priorities are ignored.
Render the first surface as a white diffuse material.
The maximum subdivision level that should be applied on the geometries in the scene. Setting zero will disable the subdivision.
Keeps environment with enabled alpha channel.
The action to be taken on selected lights IDs.
Globally enable or disable light IDs. A combination of flags in the LightPassMask enum.
Inverts the light linking behavior for selected light IDs. A combination of flags in the LightPassMask enum.

String.Text: The scramble file to load. If not valid, Octane falls back to the embedded scrambling.
Path may get terminated when ray power is less than this value.
Specifies the number of direct light rays traced for every sample. This amount is used after camera rays, and after very smooth specular reflections or transmission.
Runs the kernel more coherently which makes it usually faster, but may require at least a few hundred samples/pixel to get rid of visible artifacts.
If enabled, the noise patterns are kept stable between frames.

Specifies the number of samples that are run in parallel. A small number means less parallel samples and less memory usage, but potentially slower speed. A large number means more memory usage and potentially a higher speed.
The maximum samples we calculate until we switch to a new tile.
If enabled, the work is distributed to the network render nodes in such a way to minimize the amount of data that is sent to the network render master.
Stops rendering clean parts of the image and focuses on noisy parts.
A pixel treated as noisy pixel if noise level is higher than this threshold. Only valid if the adaptive sampling or the noise render pass is enabled.

Minimum number of samples per pixel until adaptive sampling kicks in. Set it to a higher value if you notice that the error estimate is incorrect and stops sampling pixels too early resulting in artifacts.\nOnly valid if adaptive sampling is enabled.
Size of the pixel groups that are evaluated together to decide whether sampling should stop or not.

The expected exposure should be approximately the same value as the exposure in the imager or 0 to ignore this settings.\nIt's used by adaptive sampling to determine which pixels are bright and which are dark, which obviously depends on the exposure setting in the imaging settings. Adaptive sampling tweaks/reduces the noise estimate of very dark areas of the image. It also increases the min. adaptive samples limit for very dark areas which tend to find paths to light sources only very irregularly and thus have a too optimistic noise estimate.
Specifies how many surfaces should be skipped by the ray before starting sampling.
Specifies the ray offset when a surface is skipped due to surface peeling.
Specifies which primitive faces are displayed

Controls the appearance of colors produced by spectral emitters (e.g. daylight environment, black body emitters). This determines the spectrum that will produce white (before white balance) in the final image. Use D65 to adapt to a reasonable daylight "white" color. Use Legacy/flat to preserve the appearance of old projects (spectral emitters will appear rather blue).
Include render AOVs in deep pixels.
Maximum number of depth samples per pixels.
Depth samples whose relative depth difference falls below the tolerance value are merged together.
The ambient modifier of toon shadowing.
The percentage of roughness affecting subsequent layers' roughness.
The strength for dynamic AI light update.
(deprecated) Runs the kernel more coherently which makes it usually faster, but may require at least a few hundred samples/pixel to get rid of visible artifacts.
(deprecated) The strength with which the adaptive sampling is applied. Lower the values will increase render time. Only valid if adaptive sampling is enabled.
(deprecated) Emulate the behavior of emission and scattering of version 4.0 and earlier.

(deprecated) Use the old behavior for converting colors to and from spectra and for applying white balance. Use this to preserve the appearance of old projects (textures with colors outside the sRGB gamut will be rendered inaccurately).
Specifies the maximum area affected by the dirt effect.
Determines the proportion of the maximum area affected by the dirt effect.

Spread controls the ray direction with respect to the normal of the surface. 0 means the dirt direction is shot straight in the direction of the surface normal, and 1 means the dirt rays are shot in all directions in the upper hemisphere in a cosine lobe.
Distribution controls how evenly rays are shot within the sampling cone. When the value is 100, rays gather closer to the lateral surface. If the value is 1 rays are evenly distributed.

The shading normal vector in shading space that we sample with as a custom direction. By default the direction is (0, 0, 1), which is the shading normal in shading coordinates. If any non-zero bias is set, then this bias vector is used as shading normal to sample dirt rays.
The coordinate space the bias vector is in.

Includes objects when calculating dirt value: By default the selected mode is All, which includes all object intersections into calculating dirt. If Self is selected, then only self-intersection is taken into account for dirt. If Others is selected, then only ray-intersection with other objects is used for dirt.
The name that was used to save the image, in a layer below this one. The saved image can't be loaded again later, but more GPU memory will be available for subsequent compositor operations.
The value in the image which corresponds to zero displacement. The range is always normalized to [0, 1].
Level of detail, i.e. the resolution of the internal displacement map.
The surface will be displaced along the given direction.
Specifies which filter type to use on the displacement map texture.
Number of nearest pixels to use for filtering. The higher the value the smoother the displacement map. Only valid if a filter is enabled.
Additional offset applied to allow moving the displaced surface.
The emission texture (on the emitting surface).
Scale factor applied to the emission.

If enabled, this node determines emitted power per 7 / pi units of surface area, so the total emitted power will be proportional to the area of the surface. If disabled, this node determines total emitted power, regardless of the area of the surface.
If enabled and "Surface brightness" is off, then the power remains constant if uniform scaling is applied to the instance.
If enabled, the emitter will emit from the front side as well as from the back side.
Normalize the luminous power of the blackbody emitter, i.e. make it independent of the temperature.
The directional emission pattern of the light source.
Indicates how often this light source should be sampled. 1 is the default value, 0 means this light source is not sampled directly.
ID of the light pass that captures the contribution of this emitter.
If enabled, the light source casts light and shadows onto diffuse surfaces.
If enabled, the light source is visible on specular surfaces.
If enabled, the light source is visible on scattering volumes.
Light source casts illumination on diffuse objects even if the emitter is transparent.
If enabled (which is the default), direct light shadows are calculated for this light source. This applies only to emitters with a sampling rate > 0.
The value of the enum node.

The falloff mode that should be used:

'Normal vs. eye ray': The falloff is calculated from the angle between the surface normal and the eye ray.
'Normal vs. vector 90deg': The falloff is calculated from the angle between the surface normal and the specified direction vector maxing out at 90 degrees.
'Normal vs vector 180deg': The falloff is calculated from the angle between the surface normal and the specified direction vector maxing out at 180 degrees.

If enabled, the shading normal, which includes bump/normal mapping, will be used to calculate the falloff. If disabled, the smooth normal which does not include bump/normal mapping, will be used instead.
Value if the angle between the two directions is 0.
Value if the angle between the two directions is at the maximum.
Skew factor for the falloff curve.
The direction vector that is used by some of the falloff modes.
Distance at which the value falls down to zero.
Offset applied to the core shape surface at which the value starts falling off from one.
Signed distance field representing the shape inside which the value is one.
The absolute start coordinate where the render region starts in pixels. This input determines the actual start of the render region.
The absolute size of the render region in pixels. This input determines the actual size of the render region.
The relative start coordinate where the render region starts in percent. This input exists only to control the absolute region start in pixels, but is not used directly in the render settings.
The relative size of the render region in percent. This input exists only to control the absolute region size in pixels, but is not used directly in the render settings.

If enabled, and the film resolution is changed, the relative film region stays constant and the absolute film region in pixels gets updated.\n\nIf disabled, and the film resolution is changed, the absolute film region in pixels stays constant and the relative film region gets updated.
The background color. Ignored if the texture is used as a normal map.
The base size of the flakes.
Determines how much flakes vary in size.
Blend between the distorted normal / flake color (0.0) and the undistorted normal / background color (1.0).
The value of the float node.
The value of the float texture node.
Offset applied to the frame index. The frame index normally starts at 0 for the first frame. The default offset is 1, making it suitable to be used as an index source for switch nodes.
Name of the group this linker node belongs to. The group is used in the node inspector to group inputs, similar to the groups specified in node pin infos.
The number of inputs. Any new input will be added to the end of the list.
The number of geometry input pins. Any new inputs will be added to the end of the pin list.

Stores the CSV file to load the transforms from. After loading successfully the A_TRANSFORMS and A_USER_INSTANCE_IDS attributes will be replaced by the file contents, otherwise the A_TRANSFORMS and AT_FILENAME and A_USER_INSTANCE_IDS attributes are reverted to their original value.

String.Text: Defines the length unit used to create the transform matrices. This applies to the rightmost column of the transform matrix, which defines the translation component. (see Octane::GeometryImportScale)

The transforms stored in this node.\n This array may contain matrices set to 0, those are entries which are invisible in the current frame. This can be useful for motion blur and random object color textures.
If enabled the transforms are relative to the object space of the destination node, otherwise they are absolute transforms from world space to object space.

An array of identifiers for the instances, The instance IDs are assigned to transform nodes in the array index order. If this array is empty and for any unassigned instances, IDs are set to invalid. A valid ID should be a non-negative number. It's a non-unique ID, multiple nodes can have the same ID, so it's a user responsibility to set unique ID if needed. In a tree hierarchy, the ID of current node will override the input geometry node's ID

String.Text: Specular reflection channel which behaves like a coating on top of the diffuse layer.
Roughness of the specular reflection channel.
The anisotropy of the specular material, -1 is horizontal and 1 is vertical, 0 is isotropy.
Rotation of the anisotropic specular reflection channel.
The spread of the tail of the specular BSDF model (STD only) of the specular layer.
Thickness of the film coating in micrometers.
Index of refraction of the film coating.
The sheen color of the material.
Index of refraction controlling the Fresnel effect of the specular reflection.
If enabled, the photon tracing kernel will create caustics for light reflecting or transmitting through this object.
Displacement channel to create highly detailed geometry with a low memory footprint.
Number of times the gradient is repeated.
Number of sides to the polygon when using the polygonal gradient type.
Determines the gradient behavior for repetitions.
The number of control points between start and end.
Determines how the ratios of the input colors vary between control points.

The color space in which colors are combined between control points.

Physical uses scene-linear values and creates gradients that approximate optical effects in the real world. Perceptual uses the Oklab color space and creates gradients that vary smoothly to the human eye.

Physical should be used for textures that contain non-color data, like normals.
The texture used to address the gradient map.
(deprecated) Make the gradient more smooth around the control points.
Input value for this control point.
Output value for this control point.
The weights applied to the RGB input to calculate the grayscale output.
The absolute quantity of pigment that gives the hair base color.
The extent of redness of a hair strand.
Roughness along a hair strand for longitudinal scattering.
Roughness used for cross section of a hair strand for azimuth scattering.
Scale offset on the surface of the hair. 0 denotes perfectly smooth cylindrical hair, increasing the value shifts the specular highlight away from perfectly reflective direction.
Controls the frequency of randomness on hair.
Controls the offset of randomness on hair.
Controls the intensity of randomness on each hair strand.
Controls the target random albedo on the hair, this only works with albedo mode enabled.
Adds random roughness on top of the base roughness.
The color space of the image.
Select output channels type of this node. Can be set to one of enum ChannelGroups.
Stores the filename of the texture image.
TRUE if the file needs a reload or the preference of the image file has been changed.After evaluation the attribute will be false again.

If true, an initial color space has previously been automatically selected, and so one will not be selected again. If false, the color space will be set the next time an image is loaded. This also applies to the premultiplied alpha pin if there is one.
The resolution stored in the node. X and Y need to be > 0, Z is ignored.
The preset chosen by the user - used only by the standalone UI, since many resolutions have multiple entries in the resolution menu.
The aspect ratio width/height or 0 if the aspect ratio is not locked. Needs to be >= 0.

The exposure or overall brightness. The required value is highly dependent on the lighting of the scene. Outdoor scenes in daylight work well with an exposure between 0.6 and 1. Indoor scenes - even during the day - often need an exposure of 4 to 20.
Make pixels that are partially transparent (alpha > 0) fully opaque.
Minimum number of samples before the first image is displayed.
Maximum interval between imaging operations (in seconds).
OCIO view to use when displaying in the render viewport.
OCIO look to apply when displaying in the render viewport, if using an OCIO view.

Whether to apply Octane's built-in tone mapping (before applying any OCIO look(s)) when using an OCIO view. This may produce undesirable results due to an intermediate reduction to the sRGB color space.
Use the ACES 1.3 RRT + sRGB ODT. If this is enabled, all other tone mapping settings will be ignored.
Reduces burned out highlights by compressing them and reducing their contrast.
Controls if clipping is done per channel or not.
The order in which camera response curve, gamma and custom LUT are applied.
Camera response curve provided by Octane.
If enabled, the selected camera response curve will not affect the colors.

Gamma correction, which is applied additionally to the camera response curve. Please note that the camera response curves themselves already do a gamma correction, i.e. a gamma of 1 should be used unless you are using the response curve "Linear/off".
If set, the custom LUT is applied in the order as specified in "Order".

Turns on the denoising feature. Depending on the chosen denoising method, it cleans up the main beauty AOV and a few other beauty AOVs (specifically with the Octane denoiser), and then saves the result in separate passes.
The denoising method to utilize for reducing noise.
Whether the Octane spectral AI denoiser will denoise volumes in the scene.

Only valid for the Open Image Denoise type. If enabled, it internally pre-filters the albedo and normal AOVs before denoising the beauty AOV. Enabling this may improve the output quality if your albedo and normal AOVs are noisy, but will also increase the time required to complete the denoising process.
If enabled, beauty AOVs will be denoised only once at the end of a render. This option should be disabled while rendering with an interactive region.
Minimum number of samples per pixel until denoiser kicks in. Only valid when the denoise once option is disabled.
Maximum interval between denoiser runs (in seconds). Only valid when the denoise once option is disabled.

A value between 0 to 1 to blend the original image into the denoiser output. Setting 0 results with fully denoised image and setting 1 results with the original image. An intermediate value will produce a blend between the denoised image and the original image.
The upsampler mode used during the rendering.
Uses AI to upsample the frame when this toggle is on. Otherwise we just trivially scale up the frame.
If enabled, beauty passes will only use upsampler once at the end of a render.
Minimum number of samples per pixel until the upsampler kicks in. Only valid when the upsampler is enabled.

(deprecated) If enabled, gamma will be applied before the camera response. This is technically incorrect, but was the behaviour in version 2 and we introduced this option to be able to render older scenes without changing colors. The default (and correct) behaviour is to apply gamma last, by disabling this option.
(deprecated) Maximum interval between upsampler runs (in seconds). Only valid when the upsampler is enabled.
Gamma value. Only used when the color space is set to "Linear sRGB + legacy gamma".

String.Text: The type of Cryptomatte render AOV from which to extract mattes.

List of selected matte names, one per line.

Some characters have special meaning:
 * is a wildcard that matches any sequence of characters.
 - at the start of a line excludes any mattes matched by that line.
 ? on a line by itself matches mattes with blank names.
 \ prevents the next character being treated as a special character.

Blank lines are ignored. When a matte name is included by one line and excluded by another, whichever line comes last takes precedence. For example,
 Car_*
 -*dirt*
 Car_wheel_dirt
will include "Car_windows" and "Car_wheel_dirt", but not "Ground" or "Car_door_dirt".

Controls how quickly the eye distance gets reduced towards the poles. This is to reduce eye strain at the poles when the panorama is looked at in an HMD. A value of 1 will reduce the eye distance more or less continuously from equator to the poles, which will create a relaxed viewing experience, but this will also cause flat surfaces to appear curved. A value smaller than 1 keeps the eye distance more or less constant for a larger latitude range above and below the horizon, but will then rapidly reduce the eye distance near the poles. This will keep flat surface flat, but cause more eye strain near the poles (which can be reduced again by setting the pano cutoff latitude to something < 90 degrees).

The minimum brightness of a pixel to have bloom and glare applied. The brightness is measured after the application of the exposure.\n\nIncreasing this value will decrease the overall brightness of bloom and glare, which can be compensated by increasing the bloom/glare power, but that's scene dependent.

If enabled, bloom and glare will scale with film size. If disabled, the size of bloom and glare features will be the same number of pixels regardless of film size. This should only be disabled to match the behavior of previous versions of Octane.

To maintain the same result when enabling this, find the image length in pixels (which is film width or film height, whichever is larger), and set the following values:
 Spread start = 0.6 * sqrt(2) / image length
 Spread end = 614.4 * sqrt(2) / image length
 Spectral shift = old spectral shift + log2(image length)

Too large a value will produce an overly blurry result without fine details. Too small a value will reduce the maximum possible strength of the bloom/glare.

ID of the active render layer.
All the non-active render layers become the active render layer and the active render layer becomes inactive.

The render mode that should be used to render layers:

'Normal': The beauty passes contain the active layer only and the render layer passes (shadows, reflections...) record the side-effects of the active render layer for those samples/pixels that are not obstructed by the active render layer.
Beauty passes will be transparent for those pixels which are covered by objects on the inactive layers, even if there is an object on the active layer behind the foreground object.

'Hide inactive layers': All geometry that is not on an active layer will be made invisible. No side effects will be recorded in the render layer passes, i.e. the render layer passes will be empty.

'Only side effects': Similar to 'normal', with the exception that the active layer will be made invisible to the camera, i.e. the beauty passes will be empty. The render layer passes (shadows, reflections...) still record the side-effects of the active render layer.
This is useful to capture all side-effects without having the active layer obstructing those.
'Hide from camera': Similar to RENDER_LAYER_MODE_HIDE_INACTIVE_LAYERs All geometry that is not on an active layer will be made invisible. But side effects(shadows, reflections...)will be recorded in the render layer passes.
The layers only affect visibility i.e. objects on the non-active layer are treated as if they are not in the scene at all. Render layer passes don't work if this option is enabled.
Make the beauty pass raw render passes by dividing out the color of the BxDF of the surface hit by the camera ray.

The method used to distribute instances on surfaces.
- One instance per vertex: an instance is placed at each vertex.
- One instance per edge: an instance is placed on each edge using the position value.
- Evenly spaced instances on edges: instances are placed along edges using the position and spacing values.
- One instance per polygon: an instance is placed at the centroid of each polygon.
- Random instances by relative area: instances are placed uniformly over the surface.
- Random instances by relative density: the relative density of instances is controlled by a map.
- Disabled: no instances are placed on the surface.
The method used to select between source objects for each instance.
Seed used to randomize the selection of source objects.
Map used to associate each instance with a source object.
The method used to distribute instances on particles.\n- One instance per particle: an instance is attached to each particle.\n- Disabled: no instances are attached to particles.

The method used to distribute instances on hair strands.
- One instance per hair vertex: an instance is placed at each vertex of each hair strand.
- One instance per hair: an instance is placed on each hair strand using the position value.
- Evenly spaced instances on hair: instances are placed along hair strands using the position and spacing values.
- Disabled: no instances are placed on hair strands.
When scattering on edges this defines the position of instances along the edge.
When scattering on edges this defines the spacing between instances along the edge.
When randomly scattering on the surface by area or relative density, enabling this option distributes the instances so that no two instances are too close to each other.
When scattering on surfaces by relative density, this texture controls the relative density of instances.
When scattering on hair strands this defines the position of instances along the hair.
When scattering on hair strands this defines the spacing between instances.
Global seed used to randomize instance placement.
When instances are not attached to discrete geometry elements this defines the maximum number of instances to create.
Map used to reduce the density of instances over the surface. Instances in darker areas are more likely to be removed.
All instances in areas of the map that have a value below this threshold are removed.
All instances in areas of the map that have a value above this threshold are removed.
All instances on surfaces with a normal too close to the reference up vector are removed.
All instances on surfaces with a normal too far from the reference up vector are removed.
Values towards 0 align the instance with the reference up direction, values towards 1 align it with the default normal.
Values towards 0 align the instance with the reference front direction, values towards 1 align it with the default front.
If the up and front vector are not orthogonal this option selects which one has priority.
Selects between the use of a reference direction or a reference point.
When up mode is set to Direction, the reference up vector will point in this direction.
When up mode is set to Point, the reference up vector will point towards this location.
When front mode is set to Direction, the reference front vector will point in this direction.
When front mode is set to Point, the reference front vector will point towards this location.
When the rotation mode is random or map and this value is different from zero the values will be aliased to the nearest step.

Change how the reflectivity is calculated:

Stores the geometry file to load the Gaussian splat cloud from. Currently only PLY files that contain Gaussian splats data are supported. The PLY file is required to have the following properties in the "vertex" element: x, y, z, f_dc_0, f_dc_1, f_dc_2, opacity, scale_0, scale_1, scale_2, rot_0, rot_1, rot_2, rot_3. The extra spherical harmonics properties are optional: f_rest*. To load a new file, just change this attribute and evaluate the node. After the evaluation the geometry attributes have been replaced. If the loading fails, A_FILENAME and all geometry attributes will be reset to their value of the last successful evaluation

The way Gaussian splat cloud points are culled by clipping bounds.

'None': no points are culled.
'Box': points outside the specified clipping box primitive will be excluded from rendering.
'Ellipsoid': points outside the specified clipping ellipsoid primitive will be excluded from rendering.

Transformation applied to the clipping primitive (either box or ellipsoid).\nE.g. setting scale to (10, 10, 10) will make a clipping primitive with dimensions (10, 10, 10) centered at the origin of Gaussian splat cloud local space.
Color of the clip primitive bounds wireframe. The wireframe along the boundaries helps with aligning the clipping primitive in 3D space. You can enable this feature from the render view settings.

The priority used to determine whether clipping material should clip this Gaussian splat cloud.\nClipping materials with lower or equal priority will be ignored.\nNote: intersection material is not supported when clipping Gaussian splats.
Color tint for the Gaussian splats.
Regions of the Gaussian splats with alpha smaller than this will be invisible. Setting it to higher values will produce better performance but worse visual quality.
Bias added to the Gaussian splats scale. Increase it to make thin lines such as text more clearly visible. Note: it may negatively affect rendering performance.
Scale multiplier of the Gaussian splats.
The Gaussian splats color will be multiplied by this value.
Inverts the Gaussian splat X and Y axes (scale by -1).
When set to non-zero, Gaussian splats will simulate shadows from the light sources. Larger values will produce darker shadow. Setting it to 0 effectively disables shadows.
Offset that's added to the shadow ray position when tracing Gaussian splat shadows. Can be used to adjust the look of self-shadowing Gaussian splats.

The way Gaussian splats interact with lights.

'None': Gaussian splat brightness will not be scaled by the emitter power. Note: shadows from mesh emitters are not supported in this mode.
'Power': Gaussian splat brightness will be scaled by the emitter power and dimmed with distance to the light.
'Power and color': Gaussian splat brightness will be scaled by the emitter power and dimmed with distance to the light. Additionally, it will be tinted by the light color.

Pattern used to get a file name for a tile.

The render engine ignores this attribute, but it allows a user interface to reliably offer an interface to select tiles. The format is defined below so that it is consistent between plug-ins and Standalone.

Patterns contain placeholders: <U> and <V> for indices across the two grid dimensions, <I> for linear row major index, and <UDIM> for row major index starting at 1001. To pad indices with zeros, repeat the letter, eg. <UUU> will generate "000", "001", etc.

If you set a list of files manually you should clear this attribute. If you set this attribute to a non-empty string you should ensure the A_FILENAME attribute contains matching file names.
Flip the tile order in the V direction

A tile set is an image split into multiple tiles on a regular grid. The entire image is mapped onto one UV unit square, in the same way as regular image texture nodes. All tiles must have the same size, except for tiles along the borders, which may be more narrow.
Only used with Open Image Denoise. Sets the denoising filter quality mode. This is a trade-off between performance and image quality.
The upsample source percentage per side.

A UV tiles texture consists of multiple images, and each of these images is assigned to one unit tile in UV space. The first tile is mapped to (0, 0)-(1, 1). For directional textures (environemnt and light distribution) the entire tile grid is mirrored in UV space around its centre line, as determined by the width of the UV grid.\n\nWhen using a virtual texture, all tiles must have the same size.

This is required because Octane needs to be able to check whether some mesh data has been compiled to meshlets already or not and what the corresponding cache file is, but plugins can't really guarantee that the mesh data will be *exactly* the same between sessions.
To give maximum flexibility, the ID is a string. Since the ID will be used in the name of the meshlet cache file, it's recommended to only use characters that can be used file names. It should also not be too long for that same reason.
Import preferences are taken into account additionally to the meshlet mesh ID, i.e. two mesh nodes with the same meshlet mesh ID but different import preferences will have two different meshlet cache files.

Comma-separated list of names of trace sets that the object is a member of.

If the text starts with a hyphen, the object will be a member of all trace sets except the ones listed. Setting this to simply "-" means that the object is a member of all trace sets.

Comma-separated list of names of trace sets to be treated as invisible for future hits in light paths that hit this object.

Any object that is a member of any of these trace sets will be excluded. For example, setting this to "grass,ball" on a mirror object means any objects that are members of the "grass" or "ball" trace sets (or both) will not be reflected in the mirror.

If the text starts with a hyphen, all objects will be excluded unless they are a member of any of the listed trace sets. For example, setting this to "-grass,ball" on a mirror object means any objects that are members of neither the "grass" trace set nor the "ball" trace set (including objects that are not members of any trace sets) will not be reflected in the mirror. Setting this to simply "-" means that all objects will be excluded.

A trace set name can be any text that does not contain a comma. Spaces are ignored at the start and end of trace set names, and empty trace set names are ignored. Trace set names are case-sensitive.

Comma-separated list of names of trace sets to be treated as visible again for future hits in light paths that hit this object, after potentially having been excluded by an earlier bounce.

For example, if a cube is excluded by a mirror, but reincluded by a metal ball, the cube will not be visible in the mirror (or the mirror's reflection in the metal ball), but will still be visible in the metal ball's reflection in the mirror.

All trace sets listed will be no longer excluded. If the text starts with a hyphen, all trace sets except the ones listed will be no longer excluded (and all objects that are not members of any trace sets will be no longer excluded). Note that a trace set being no longer excluded does not necessarily mean that all objects that are members of that trace set will be no longer excluded, because those objects could also be a member of a different trace set that is still excluded.

Setting this to simply "-" means that all objects will be no longer excluded.

For each rule, reinclusions are applied after exclusions. This means reinclusions take priority if there is any conflict between the two.

A trace set name can be any text that does not contain a comma. Spaces are ignored at the start and end of trace set names, and empty trace set names are ignored. Trace set names are case-sensitive.

How this rule should take effect in the future of the light path.

"All future hits" is the simplest value, and means that after a bounce to which this rule applies, this rule will update trace set visibility for the light path.

"Next hit only" means that this rule only applies when considering the next hit after the current bounce, and the future of the light path after that will be as if this rule did not apply. For example, this can be used to exclude an object from direct reflections without changing anything for indirect reflections (an alternative may be to manually reinclude the relevant trace sets on all the indirect reflectors). This mimics the behavior of some other renderers and is primarily provided for users familiar with that behavior.

"All future hits after next hit" is the opposite of "Next hit only", and means that this rule only applies when considering the future of the light path after the next hit, and trace set visibility for the next hit itself will be as if this rule did not apply. For example, this can be used to exclude an object from indirect reflections without changing anything for direct reflections (an alternative may be to manually exclude the relevant trace sets on all the indirect reflectors).

Note that shadow bounces only continue for a single hit after the bounce, so for shadow bounces there is no difference between "All future hits" and "Next hit only", and a rule that only applies to "All future hits after next hit" will never apply to a shadow bounce.
Which original input image to extract from the blended result.

The required amount of foreground/background separation that the extracted image must have.

This should be set to 100% unless that causes artifacts due to the foreground mask having large flat areas of partial opacity - in that case this should be lowered to match the opacity of those large flat areas. Lowering this will allow artifact-free output at the cost of not fully extrapolating the background and foreground. Increasing the nearby radius may be a better approach if the flat areas are not very large.

If this is zero, unblend will behave like a regular mask operation.

This is not used if a background is provided or foreground mask source is set to "No mask (full RGBA)".

The original background that was used when creating the blended result. If this is provided, extracting the foreground is a much simpler operation that produces a more accurate result, so it should be provided when available.
